title: Ternary Search on a Unimodal Function
directAnswer: Find the peak (or valley) of a unimodal function — one that strictly increases then strictly decreases (or the reverse). You can't binary-search on the value, but you can binary-search on the slope: probe two interior points m1 < m2. If f(m1) < f(m2) the maximum is to the right of m1, so discard [lo, m1]; otherwise discard [m2, hi]. Each step removes a third of the range, giving O(log n) probes. A cleaner equivalent keeps a binary search comparing f(mid) with f(mid+1).

remember.pattern: Binary search on the derivative's sign over a unimodal range
remember.formula:
MAX of unimodal:
while hi - lo > 2:
    m1 = lo + (hi - lo) / 3
    m2 = hi - (hi - lo) / 3
    if f(m1) < f(m2): lo = m1 + 1   # peak is right of m1
    else: hi = m2 - 1               # peak is left of m2
answer = best f over [lo..hi]

DISCRETE shortcut: compare f(mid) vs f(mid+1) to decide which half holds the peak.
rules: The function must be **strictly unimodal** — one peak (or one valley), no flat plateaus. Ternary search breaks on flats because `f(m1) == f(m2)` gives no direction.
You're searching on the **shape (slope), not the value** — there's no target to match, you're locating the turning point.
For a **maximum**: `f(m1) < f(m2)` ⇒ still climbing, discard the left third; else discard the right third. Flip both comparisons for a **minimum**.
On integers, stop when the window is tiny (≤ 2–3 elements) and scan the rest, or use the `f(mid)` vs `f(mid+1)` slope test to avoid rounding traps.
On reals, iterate a fixed number of times (e.g. ~100/200) or until the interval is within epsilon — don't loop on exact equality.
whenToUse: Optimize a single-peaked / single-valley function (maximize or minimize)
Peak in a bitonic / mountain array
Geometry: minimize distance to a point along a parametrized path
Any cost function known to be convex/concave over the search range
antiSignals: Function is monotonic (only increasing or only decreasing) → plain binary search, not ternary
Function has multiple peaks / not unimodal → ternary search gives a wrong local answer
Plateaus exist (equal values over a stretch) → the comparison can't pick a side; rethink the model
You're matching a target value, not finding an extremum → ordinary binary search
remember.takeaway: Ternary search is binary search applied to the *slope* of a unimodal function: each comparison of two interior probes tells you which way is uphill, letting you throw away a constant fraction of the range every step for O(log n) convergence to the extremum.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that an extremum (not a target) over a unimodal range is still a logarithmic search, and whether you can justify which side to discard from a two-point comparison.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Applying ternary/binary search to a function that isn't strictly unimodal (plateaus or multiple peaks), or discarding the wrong third by mixing up the max vs min comparison direction.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the unimodality precondition explicitly, derive the discard rule from 'which way is uphill', and mention the cleaner f(mid) vs f(mid+1) slope binary search for the discrete case.

problemStatement:
You are given access to a **unimodal** function `f` over an index range `[0, n−1]` (or a real interval `[lo, hi]`): `f` strictly increases up to a single peak, then strictly decreases. Return the position of the maximum (the peak) and/or its value.

For a unimodal valley (strictly decreasing then increasing), return the minimum instead.
constraints: f is strictly unimodal over the search range (exactly one turning point, no plateaus)
1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁹ for the discrete version; reals use a fixed iteration count
Evaluating f is O(1) (or counted as one query)
For arrays, the peak is strictly greater than its neighbors
understanding: There's no value to match — you're hunting the single turning point of a curve that goes up then down. Because the function has just one peak, comparing the heights at two interior points reveals which side of them the peak lies on, so you can safely discard a chunk of the range each step, mirroring binary search but on the function's slope rather than on a sorted value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the function guaranteed strictly unimodal?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Critical. Ternary search is only correct with exactly one peak and no flat regions. If there are plateaus or multiple peaks, the comparison can point the wrong way.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Maximum or minimum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either — the structure is identical; you just flip the comparison direction. Confirm which extremum is wanted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Discrete indices or a real interval?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Decides the stopping rule: integers stop at a tiny window (and scan it); reals iterate a fixed number of times or until within epsilon.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is querying f expensive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If each evaluation is costly, prefer the f(mid) vs f(mid+1) binary search — it makes one comparison per step instead of two probes.

approaches.name: Linear Scan
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to fix correctness and the unimodality assumption, then point out it ignores the structure that lets us go logarithmic.
hints: Walk every position and keep the best value seen. For a peak, track the running maximum and its index.
This works for any function, unimodal or not — but it never uses the single-peak structure.
n evaluations of f. If n is large or f is expensive, this is the cost we want to cut to O(log n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n positions, one f-evaluation each → O(n). Constant bookkeeping → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The baseline simply evaluates the function everywhere and remembers the best.

**The literal method.** Iterate over all `n` positions (or sample the real interval finely), evaluate `f`, and keep the maximum value and its index.

**Why it's correct but wasteful.** It makes no assumption about shape, so it always works — but it throws away the one fact that matters here: the function has a single peak. With that structure, you don't need to look at every point; comparing a couple of interior points already tells you where the peak can't be. The linear scan ignores that and pays `O(n)` queries.

**When it's still the right call.** If `n` is small, or you're unsure the function is truly unimodal, the scan is the safe choice — ternary search silently misbehaves on non-unimodal input, while the scan always returns the true global max of the sampled points.
approaches.insight: The scan's O(n) cost comes entirely from not using unimodality. The whole optimization is to convert 'where is the max?' into repeated 'which way is uphill?' questions, each of which eliminates a fraction of the range.

dryRun.intro: Track the running maximum across all indices.

java.explanation: Track the running maximum index — works for any array, ignores unimodality.

python.explanation: Keep the index of the largest value seen so far.

pitfalls: Treating O(n) as fine when n is 10⁹ or f is expensive.
Assuming the scan needs unimodality — it doesn't, which is exactly why it's slower.
Comparing values instead of indices when the peak index is what's asked.

approaches.name: Ternary Search (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Frame it as binary search on the slope and state the unimodality precondition up front.
hints: You can't compare f to a target — there isn't one. But you can compare f at two interior points. If the function is rising between them, the peak is to the right; if falling, the peak is to the left.
Split [lo, hi] into thirds with m1 = lo + (hi-lo)/3 and m2 = hi - (hi-lo)/3. Compare f(m1) and f(m2) to discard one outer third each step.
For integers, a cleaner variant binary-searches by comparing f(mid) with f(mid+1): if f(mid) < f(mid+1) the peak is to the right (lo = mid+1), else to the left (hi = mid).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each step removes about a third of the range (ternary) or half (the slope binary search), so the number of iterations is O(log n). Each iteration does O(1) f-evaluations → O(log n) total queries, O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Ternary search locates the extremum of a unimodal function by repeatedly asking which direction is uphill.

**Why you can't binary-search the value.** Ordinary binary search needs a sorted/monotone relationship to a target. Here the values rise then fall, and there's no target — you want the turning point. So instead of comparing `f(mid)` to a target, you compare the function at two points to read its slope.

**The two-probe step.** Pick interior points `m1 = lo + (hi−lo)/3` and `m2 = hi − (hi−lo)/3`, so `m1 < m2`. Evaluate both. For a **maximum**:
- If `f(m1) < f(m2)`, the function is still climbing as you go from `m1` to `m2`, which means the peak lies to the right of `m1`. Discard `[lo, m1]` by setting `lo = m1 + 1`.
- Otherwise (`f(m1) >= f(m2)`), you're already on the descending side by `m2`, so the peak is to the left of `m2`. Discard `[m2, hi]` by setting `hi = m2 − 1`.

Either way you throw away roughly a third of the range. Repeat until the window is tiny, then take the best point in it. For a **minimum**, flip both comparisons.

**The cleaner discrete variant.** On integer indices, two probes per step invite off-by-one and rounding bugs. A simpler equivalent is a binary search on the slope: take `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` and compare `f(mid)` with `f(mid+1)`. If `f(mid) < f(mid+1)` the slope is positive, so the peak is to the right: `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise the peak is at `mid` or to its left: `hi = mid`. When `lo == hi`, that index is the peak. This halves the range each step with a single comparison and no thirds arithmetic — it's the version to prefer for arrays.

**Real intervals.** With continuous `x`, you can't reach exact equality. Iterate a fixed number of times (about 100–200 doublings of precision) or until `hi − lo < epsilon`, then report the midpoint. Never loop on `f(m1) == f(m2)` exactly — floating point won't cooperate.

**The non-negotiable precondition.** All of this assumes *strict* unimodality. If the function has a flat stretch, `f(m1)` can equal `f(m2)` with the peak on either side, and the discard rule has no basis. If there are multiple peaks, you may converge to the wrong one. State this assumption out loud — it's the thing interviewers probe.
approaches.insight: Binary search exploits monotonicity to halve a search for a *value*; ternary search exploits unimodality to shrink a search for an *extremum*. Both reduce the range by a constant factor per step — the only difference is that here each comparison reads the slope (is it going up or down?) rather than checking against a target. Seeing that 'slope sign' is itself monotone over a unimodal range is what lets the simpler binary-search-on-f(mid)-vs-f(mid+1) work.

Left interior probe at the one-third mark for the real-valued version.
Rising from m1 to m2 → discard the left third by moving lo up.

python.explanation: Slope test — the discrete, off-by-one-safe form of ternary search.

python.line: lo = mid + 1   # still climbing -> peak to the right
python.explanation: Discard the left half including mid.

python.line: hi = mid        # descending -> peak at mid or left
python.explanation: Retain mid as a peak candidate.
Fixed iteration count for the real interval — converges well within float precision.

pitfalls: Using ternary search on a non-unimodal or plateaued function — the discard rule becomes invalid.
Flipping the comparison direction (max vs min) and converging on the wrong extremum.
Looping until f(m1) == f(m2) on reals — float equality may never hold; iterate a fixed count.
Off-by-one in the two-probe integer version — prefer the f(mid) vs f(mid+1) form.

commonMistakes: Applying ternary search to a function that isn't strictly unimodal (multiple peaks or plateaus).
Mixing up the comparison direction so you find a valley when you wanted a peak.
Looping on exact float equality instead of a fixed iteration count for real intervals.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Assuming unimodality that isn't there
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the function has two peaks or a flat region, comparing two probes can point toward the wrong region, and ternary search converges to a non-global point. Verify the precondition first.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# arr = [9, 7, 4, 6, 10] has two 'uphill' directions
idx = peak_index(arr)   # meaningless: not unimodal
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# Ensure strictly-up-then-down before using ternary search;
# otherwise fall back to a linear scan.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong discard direction for max vs min
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For a maximum, f(m1) < f(m2) means go right. For a minimum the logic inverts. Copy-pasting the max version to find a min silently returns the wrong extremum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Looping on float equality
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On real intervals f(m1) == f(m2) may never become exactly true, so a while loop on equality can spin forever. Use a fixed iteration count or an epsilon width.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while f(m1) != f(m2):   # may never terminate on floats
    ...
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for _ in range(200):    # fixed iterations -> well within precision
    ...

patternNote: Ternary search / binary-search-on-slope. Recognise it whenever you must optimize a single-peaked or single-valley function: probe the slope, discard a constant fraction, converge in O(log n). For discrete arrays, the f(mid) vs f(mid+1) form is the cleaner sibling.
